target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would reliably remove work-related barriers for many voters
objection: Declaring Election Day a federal or national holiday does not require private employers to close or provide paid time off, and many retail and service workers would still work; therefore, the holiday would not reliably give many working voters time away from work to vote.

target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would help low-income workers
objection: Low-income workers are disproportionately represented in private retail and service jobs, so if private employers are not required to give paid time off on a federal holiday, low-income voters may still face the same scheduling barriers; thus the holiday could disadvantage low-income workers by leaving barriers in place.

target: AG1’s argument that an Election Day holiday would meaningfully increase turnout on its own
objection: Research and comparative evidence indicate that an election holiday by itself is not an effective way to increase voter turnout compared with other voting-access reforms.

target: AG1’s suggestion that a national holiday is the best reform because it removes scheduling barriers
objection: State laws that require employer time off for voting, and automatic voter registration, are more direct and reliable ways to improve access than simply making Election Day a holiday.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday would solve childcare and school-schedule barriers for parents
objection: A federal/national holiday does not itself require schools to close or change schedules, especially private schools and many districts; therefore school-based childcare/supervision constraints would not be reliably reduced for parents.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday would especially help low-income working families through school closures
objection: Because school closures or schedule changes are not guaranteed, low-income families cannot rely on holiday status to remove their school-based supervision/childcare constraints, so the holiday would not provide a dependable childcare improvement for them.

target: AG1’s claim that reduced childcare constraints would translate into voting access for low-income parents
objection: Even if school-related supervision constraints were reduced, many low-income parents would still be working during voting hours and could not reliably use those childcare gains to vote, so the mechanism does not reliably improve access for them.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday status would reduce work-related conflicts for low-income parents
objection: A national holiday does not legally require private employers to give paid time off or wage protection; low-income hourly workers may not be able to afford missing a shift or may face discipline risk, so work barriers remain even on a holiday.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday is a reliable voting-access reform for low-income working parents
objection: If low-income workers cannot afford or safely take time off, then reductions in childcare or scheduling conflicts do not translate into reliable voting access; a holiday alone is not a dependable remedy for them.

target: AG1’s broader claim that a national holiday is the main reform needed because it addresses voting barriers
objection: A holiday primarily changes schedules, but it does not directly address administrative and logistical barriers that other reforms like automatic voter registration target, so it is less reliable than reforms that cover multiple barrier types.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday sufficiently improves access for low-income working parents via school closures
objection: Closing schools for a holiday does not eliminate the need for alternative childcare, which may be costly or unavailable for low-income families; therefore childcare/supervision constraints can remain in place.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday would reliably remove scheduling barriers for low-income workers
objection: Because low-income workers are concentrated in jobs with staffing needs that continue on holidays, many would still be working and lack guaranteed time away to vote, so the holiday would leave key barriers in place.

target: AG1’s claim that absentee/mail voting plus a holiday would solve the time problem for low-income workers
objection: Low-income workers may still lack enough free time around Election Day to complete and return absentee/mail ballots, and holiday timing can also make mail or drop-off submission harder because of reduced service hours and slower processing.
